TRUSTEE'S NOTIFICATION TO BENEFICIARIES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105

BACKGROUND INFORMATION — TRUSTEE'S NOTIFICATION TO BENEFICIARIES AND HEIRS
I, Jordan Lee, am serving, or have been asked to serve, as trustee of The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust, executed March 3, 2015, following the death of Pat Morgan on August 1, 2026. This information sheet describes California's statutory trustee-notification requirement as background in connection with The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust. My address as trustee, for purposes of any actual notification, is: 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105. This information sheet is not itself the notification a trustee must serve on a trust's beneficiaries and heirs under California Probate Code § 16061.7; preparing, reviewing, or signing it does not satisfy Jordan Lee's notice obligation, if any, for The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust or for any other trust. Only actual service of a notification that satisfies § 16061.7's required content, service method, and timing does that.

THE STATUTORY DUTY TO NOTIFY, AND THE THREE EVENTS THAT TRIGGER IT
A trustee's duty to serve the statutory notification described in this document arises only upon one of three specific events: (1) a revocable trust, or a portion of it, becomes irrevocable because of the death of one or more of its settlors, or becomes irrevocable within one year of a settlor's death because of a contingency related to that death; (2) there is a change of trustee of an irrevocable trust; or (3) a power of appointment a settlor retained becomes effective or lapses upon the settlor's death, for an inter vivos trust that was, or was purported to be, irrevocable when created — with an exception for a charitable remainder annuity trust or unitrust. Where The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust became irrevocable following Pat Morgan's death on August 1, 2026, that is an instance of the first event; the same statute imposes an identical duty for the other two events even when no settlor has just died. The duty to serve the notification belongs to the continuing or successor trustee of The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust, and if The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust has more than one trustee, any one cotrustee may serve it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A trustee shall serve a notification by the trustee as described in this section in the following events:(1) When a revocable trust or any portion thereof becomes irrevocable because of the death of one or more of the settlors of the trust, or because, by the express terms of the trust, the trust becomes irrevocable within one year of the death of a settlor because of a contingency related to the death of one or more of the settlors of the trust.(2) Whenever there is a change of trustee of an irrevocable trust.(3) Whenever a power of appointment retained by a settlor is effective or lapses upon death of the settlor with respect to an inter vivos trust which was, or was purported to be, irrevocable upon its creation. This paragraph shall not apply to a charitable remainder trust. For purposes of this paragraph, “charitable remainder trust” means a charitable remainder annuity trust or charitable remainder unitrust as defined in Section 664(d) of the Internal Revenue Code.(4) The duty to serve the notification by the trustee pursuant to this subdivision is the duty of the continuing or successor trustee, and any one cotrustee may serve the notification."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(a) (California Legislative Information text), the trustee's duty to serve notification and its three triggering events (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.7.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself satisfy any trustee's notice obligation for any specific trust — only actual, compliant service of the statutory notification does that. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: the duty to notify is not triggered by a settlor's death alone. Section 16061.7(a) lists three independent triggering events, and only one of them — irrevocability caused by, or within one year of, a settlor's death — involves a settlor's death at all; a change of trustee of an already-irrevocable trust, or the lapse of a power of appointment retained over an irrevocable inter vivos trust, each independently triggers the same duty even where no settlor has just died. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (§ 16061.7(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHO MUST RECEIVE THE NOTIFICATION — BENEFICIARIES, HEIRS, AND THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
The notification described in this document must be served on each beneficiary of the irrevocable trust or irrevocable portion of the trust (subject to the limitations of a separate Probate Code section governing notice to a person who may represent and bind another); on each heir of the deceased settlor, if the triggering event is a settlor's death or irrevocability within one year of it; and, if the trust is a charitable trust subject to the Attorney General's supervision, on the Attorney General. For determining who Pat Morgan's heirs are, a trustee may rely on any final judicial determination of heirship known to the trustee, and otherwise has discretion to make a good-faith determination by any reasonable means. A trustee need not provide the notification to a beneficiary or heir who is known to the trustee but cannot be located after reasonable diligence, or who is unknown to the trustee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(b) The notification by the trustee required by subdivision (a) shall be served on each of the following:(1) Each beneficiary of the irrevocable trust or irrevocable portion of the trust, subject to the limitations of Section 15804.(2) Each heir of the deceased settlor, if the event that requires notification is the death of a settlor or irrevocability within one year of the death of the settlor of the trust by the express terms of the trust because of a contingency related to the death of a settlor.(3) If the trust is a charitable trust subject to the supervision of the Attorney General, to the Attorney General."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(b) (California Legislative Information text), who the notification must be served on (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.7.)
  "(c) A trustee shall, for purposes of this section, rely upon any final judicial determination of heirship, known to the trustee, but the trustee shall have discretion to make a good faith determination by any reasonable means of the heirs of a deceased settlor in the absence of a final judicial determination of heirship known to the trustee."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(c) (California Legislative Information text), how a trustee determines the heirs of a deceased settlor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.7.)
  "(d) The trustee need not provide a copy of the notification by trustee to any beneficiary or heir (1) known to the trustee but who cannot be located by the trustee after reasonable diligence or (2) unknown to the trustee."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(d) (California Legislative Information text), the exception for a beneficiary or heir who cannot be located or is unknown (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.7.)

This document is informational: it does not itself satisfy any trustee's notice obligation for any specific trust, and it does not identify the actual beneficiaries or heirs of any specific decedent — only actual, compliant service of the statutory notification, addressed to the actual persons the statute requires, does that. This clause cites three different subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 16061.7(b), (c), and (d)); no single subdivision is cited more than once in this clause. The beneficiary-notice requirement is itself made 'subject to the limitations of Section 15804' — a separate Probate Code section permitting certain persons (for example, a parent representing a minor beneficiary in specified circumstances) to receive notice on another person's behalf; this document does not independently quote or fully research that representation mechanism, and does not determine whether it applies to any specific beneficiary.

THE 60-DAY DEADLINE TO SERVE THE NOTIFICATION, AND HOW IT MUST BE SERVED
The notification described in this document — including any actual notification a trustee of The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust may need to serve — must be served by one of the methods a separate Probate Code section (§ 1215) authorizes, sent to the recipient's last known address. As a general rule, it must be served not later than 60 days following the occurrence of the event that requires it. A second, separate 60-day period applies only to a person entitled to the notification who was not known to the trustee when the triggering event occurred: for that person, the deadline instead runs 60 days from the date the trustee became aware of that person's existence. If there is a vacancy in the office of trustee on the date of the triggering event, or if that event itself causes the vacancy, the 60-day period does not begin to run until the date the new trustee commences to serve as trustee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(e) The notification by trustee shall be served by any of the methods described in Section 1215 to the last known address."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(e) (California Legislative Information text), the required method of service (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.7.)
  "(f) The notification by trustee shall be served not later than 60 days following the occurrence of the event requiring service of the notification by trustee, or 60 days after the trustee became aware of the existence of a person entitled to receive notification by trustee, if that person was not known to the trustee on the occurrence of the event requiring service of the notification. If there is a vacancy in the office of the trustee on the date of the occurrence of the event requiring service of the notification by trustee, or if that event causes a vacancy, then the 60-day period for service of the notification by trustee commences on the date the new trustee commences to serve as trustee."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(f) (California Legislative Information text), the 60-day deadline, its previously-unknown-person exception, and the trustee-vacancy rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.7.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself serve any notification, and preparing it does not start, toll, or satisfy the 60-day deadline described here for any specific trust — only actual, compliant service of the statutory notification does that. This clause cites two different subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 16061.7(e) and (f)); no single subdivision is cited more than once in this clause. This confirms the assumption in the original research brief that the deadline is commonly understood as 60 days: the statute's text sets that figure directly, both for the general case and for the previously-unknown-person exception, rather than deriving it by cross-reference to some other number of days.

WHAT THE NOTIFICATION MUST CONTAIN
California Probate Code § 16061.7(g) requires the notification described in this document to contain five specific items: the identity of the settlor or settlors of The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust and the date The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust's instrument was executed; the name, address, and telephone number of each trustee of The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust, including Jordan Lee at 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105; the address of the physical location of The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust's principal place of administration; any additional information the trust instrument itself expressly requires; and a notification that the recipient is entitled, upon reasonable request to the trustee, to receive from the trustee a true and complete copy of the terms of the trust.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(g) The notification by trustee shall contain the following information:(1) The identity of the settlor or settlors of the trust and the date of execution of the trust instrument.(2) The name, address, and telephone number of each trustee of the trust.(3) The address of the physical location where the principal place of administration of the trust is located, pursuant to Section 17002.(4) Any additional information that may be expressly required by the terms of the trust instrument.(5) A notification that the recipient is entitled, upon reasonable request to the trustee, to receive from the trustee a true and complete copy of the terms of the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(g) (California Legislative Information text), the five required contents of the notification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.7.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself constitute a notification that satisfies § 16061.7(g) for any specific trust — only an actual notification containing all five required items, properly served, does that. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: the statute's required-content list has five items, not the four the brief anticipated. Beyond settlor identity and the trust's date of execution, trustee name/address/telephone, and the reasonable-request entitlement to a full copy of the trust's terms, the statute also requires the address of the trust's principal place of administration and any additional information the trust instrument itself expressly requires. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (§ 16061.7(g)); no additional independent source was found for this.

CONFIDENTIALITY OF TRUST TERMS — AVAILABLE ON REQUEST, NOT AUTOMATICALLY DISCLOSED
Neither the notification described in this document nor the statute requiring it obligates a trustee to send a copy of The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust's actual terms to every beneficiary or heir automatically. Instead, § 16061.7(g)(5) requires only that the notification tell the recipient that they are entitled, upon reasonable request to the trustee, to receive a true and complete copy of the terms of The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust from Jordan Lee — for example, if Alex Morgan makes that request. A separate statute governing a trustee's general reporting duty confirms the same 'on request' structure outside the notification context: on a beneficiary's reasonable request, a trustee must report to that beneficiary by providing information relating to the trust's administration that is relevant to the beneficiary's interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(5) A notification that the recipient is entitled, upon reasonable request to the trustee, to receive from the trustee a true and complete copy of the terms of the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(g)(5) (California Legislative Information text), the recipient is entitled to a copy only upon reasonable request (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.7.)
  "Except as provided in Section 16069, on reasonable request by a beneficiary, the trustee shall report to the beneficiary by providing requested information to the beneficiary relating to the administration of the trust relevant to the beneficiary’s interest."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061 (California Legislative Information text), the trustee's general duty to report on a beneficiary's reasonable request (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trustee notification requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document is informational: it does not itself notify anyone of anything, and it does not determine what any specific trust's terms say or who is entitled to see them — only an actual, compliant § 16061.7 notification, followed by the trustee's response (if any) to an actual reasonable request, does that. This clause quotes subdivision (g)(5) of Probate Code section 16061.7, already quoted in full as part of a separate clause of this document addressing all five required contents of the notification; it is repeated here, rather than only cross-referenced, because this clause makes a distinct point about that subdivision — that it authorizes withholding the trust's actual terms absent a request — that the required-contents clause does not itself draw out. The clause's second citation is to a different statutory section (§ 16061), not a repetition of § 16061.7.

THE MANDATORY CONTEST WARNING AND THE 120-DAY LIMITATIONS PERIOD IT DESCRIBES
When the notification described in this document is served because a trust became irrevocable due to a settlor's death (or within one year of it, under a contingency tied to that death), § 16061.7(h) requires the notification to include a specific warning, set out in a separate paragraph in at least 10-point boldface type (or a reasonable equivalent), stating: 'You may not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days from the date this notification by the trustee is served upon you or 60 days from the date on which a copy of the terms of the trust is delivered to you during that 120-day period, whichever is later.' A separate statute, § 16061.8, makes that warning an accurate statement of law for a person actually served with the notification under this trigger: that person may not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days from the date the notification is served, or 60 days from the date a copy of the trust's terms is delivered during that 120-day period, whichever is later — and this rule applies whether the notification was served within or after the ordinary 60-day service deadline described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If the notification by the trustee is served because a revocable trust or any portion of it has become irrevocable because of the death of one or more settlors of the trust, or because, by the express terms of the trust, the trust becomes irrevocable within one year of the death of a settlor because of a contingency related to the death of one or more of the settlors of the trust, the notification by the trustee shall also include a warning, set out in a separate paragraph in not less than 10-point boldface type, or a reasonable equivalent thereof, that states as follows:“You may not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days from the date this notification by the trustee is served upon you or 60 days from the date on which a copy of the terms of the trust is delivered to you during that 120-day period, whichever is later.”"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(h) (California Legislative Information text), the required boldface contest-deadline warning (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.7.)
  "A person upon whom the notification by the trustee is served pursuant to paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 16061.7, whether the notice is served on the person within or after the time period set forth in subdivision (f) of Section 16061.7, shall not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days from the date the notification by the trustee is served upon the person, or 60 days from the date on which a copy of the terms of the trust is delivered pursuant to Section 1215 to the person during that 120-day period, whichever is later."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.8 (California Legislative Information text), the 120-day/60-day limitations period on contesting the trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=16061.8.)

This document is informational: it does not itself serve any notification and does not determine the limitations period applicable to any specific person's ability to contest any specific trust — only actual, compliant service of the statutory notification, described here, starts the period this clause addresses. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: delivering a copy of the trust's terms along with, or shortly after, the notification does not shorten the 120-day period to 60 days. The statute takes 'whichever is later' of two figures — 120 days from service of the notification, or 60 days from delivery of a copy of the trust's terms during that 120-day period — so the period can only be extended beyond 120 days by a copy delivered late in that window; it is never cut below 120 days by delivering a copy sooner. This document does not resolve whether § 16061.8's 120-day bar applies to a person who is never served the notification at all: the statute's own text limits the bar to 'a person upon whom the notification by the trustee is served,' which on its face does not reach someone never served, but a search for a published California appellate decision confirming that reading returned a rate-limit error from the case-law search tool used for this research (CourtListener: '429 Rate limit exceeded, 125/day') rather than a completed search; that search was not repeated or worked around, and no case-law citation is offered on this specific point as a result. Separately, § 16061.8's 120-day bar applies, by its own terms, only to a notification served under paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of § 16061.7 — the death-of-settlor trigger — not to a notification served because of a change of trustee or a lapsed power of appointment; this document does not address what limitations period, if any, applies to a contest following those other two triggers.

A SETTLOR CANNOT WAIVE THIS NOTICE REQUIREMENT; A TRUSTEE MAY NOTIFY ADDITIONAL PERSONS
Any waiver by a settlor of the requirement that a trustee serve the notification described in this document is against public policy and void — a settlor cannot use The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust's own terms to excuse Jordan Lee, or any successor trustee, from this statutory duty. Separately, a trustee may serve the notification, in the form the statute requires, on any person in addition to those the statute requires it be served on, and is not liable to any person for serving, or for not serving, the notification on someone beyond that required group. The statute also does not require a trustee to serve a notification for a triggering event that occurred before January 1, 1998.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — TRUSTEE'S NOTIFICATION TO BENEFICIARIES INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee, as trustee of The Pat Morgan Revocable Living Trust: ☐ _________________________

It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete the notification that section requires a trustee to serve, and preparing or signing it does not satisfy that requirement, start or stop the statutory 60-day service deadline, or affect the 120-day period under Probate Code § 16061.8 in which a beneficiary or heir may contest a trust; only an actual notification, served in the manner and within the time this document describes, does that.]
